paragraphs.source_en:
Drifted along the earth-creeping breeze
Between the trunks of the great hoar trees,
10 Hangs each a pearl in the pale flowers
Of the green laurel, blown anew;
And bends, and then fades silently,
One frail and fair anenome:
Or when some star of many a one
15 That climb and wander through steep night,
Has found the cleft through which alone
Beams fall from high those depths upon,
Ere it is borne away, away,
By the swift Heavens that cannot stay —
20 It scatters drops of golden light,
Like lines of rain that ne’er unite:
And the gloom divine is all around;
And underneath is the mossy ground.

paragraphs.source_en:
that S. intends a place/time contrast, but where/where and when/when are both defensible. The formula
save where, introducing a series of parallel clauses (cp. Or when, line 14), is a stock convention in
English natural descriptive poetry; cp. Gray, ‘Elegy in a Country Churchyard’ 7–12, Collins, ‘Ode to
Evening’ 9–14.
 Drifted] A participle; ‘wafted’, ‘made to drift’. breeze] Nbk 8; breeze, 1820, 1839.
 I.e. ‘hangs a pearl in each flower’; cp. Midsummer Night’s Dream II i 14–15: ‘I must go seek some
dewdrops here/And hang a pearl in every cowslip’s ear’.
 The laurel was sacred to Apollo and traditionally associated with poets; see e.g. Faerie Queene I i 9:
‘The Laurell, meed of mightie Conquerours/And Poets sage’.
 Inverted syntax; ‘save where one anemone bends and fades . . .’
 when] See note to line 7.
 climb and wander] Nbk 8; climbs and wanders 1820, 1839; many a one (line 14) is the plural subject
